title: Liveshare is merged into the host's own multi-client surface: a share is a second kind of principal on the owner's listener
No relay: the relay protocol, the owner gateway process and relay sign-in are not built
A viewer watches and cannot act
A share is explicit, single-use, time-boxed, visible, memory-only and honest about what it shows
An owner lets one invited browser watch one session, read-only, until a stated time
A share is always visible to the owner, ends on time, and can be stopped at once
A viewer's page shows the transcript and nothing else, and the owner is told exactly what that is
Create is refused unless an owner acknowledged it within the lifetime, count and transport bounds, makes no outbound request, and shows the invitation once
The invitation exchange works once; every failure gives one identical page and no cookie; an owner browser stays the owner
Over the full route table a viewer is allowed exactly the view role's actions on the shared session and refused everything else before a handler runs
The session page rendered for a viewer has no form, composer, refused control or link to another session, and the exposure statement equals the role
Expiry under virtual time ends the stream and closes the audit row; the binding denies by the clock even if the timer has not run
Stop and stop-all are idempotent and attributed; disabling the entry through the real loader ends every share and removes routes, policy and principal kind
The owner's badge and list mark are in the baseline and follow create, join and end; a second process shows them read-only; stale rows close at start
A viewer's stream carries the journal in order, resumes by cursor, carries no interaction, shell or view events, and never wakes a session
The invitation and cookie values print redacted everywhere, and a released secret value reaches the viewer masked
A second person watches a live session in a real browser and can do nothing else
A share ends by itself: expiry, host restart, and disabling the feature
A share may be created with no expiry: an absent lifetime means the share never expires
A share at the view tier is not watch-only: the viewer prompts the shared session and stops its running turn, and no passive mode exists

reason: The need (another person watches a session live) is kept and folded into the host's ordinary multi-client surface: one default-off component adds a share-viewer principal, a one-time invitation and a read-only policy, and the session page, event stream and access decision of the route and listener areas do the rest. Not carried over: the relay registration and gateway worker, owner sign-in at the relay, the two driving tiers, forks and their tool ceilings, viewer uploads and the plugin-method picker.

The package holds what the owner bundle and the separately deployed relay must agree on: owner-to-worker frames, gateway frames, the carrier script injected into the relayed page, and the relay's identity contract. The Go design has no relay and no relayed client application: the viewer's browser is a client of the owner's host, so no frame, carrier or identity contract remains. The viewer-state vocabulary shrinks to one refusal page and the ordinary problem page.

The package runs the whole JavaScript host inside a browser Web Worker for the no-install Preview, per-pull-request previews and a packaging regression test. The owner dropped the in-browser runtime: a Go host could only do this as a WebAssembly build, a second target with its own storage, sandbox and network answers. No replacement is designed; section 3.4 of the specification records what is given up.

The package is the build tool that packs built JavaScript packages into the file-system image the browser worker mounts. With the in-browser runtime dropped there is no image to pack, and a Go binary already links every component, so nothing of the packer has a counterpart.

ctx.liveshareShares (twelve owner-only remote methods) is replaced by the service key sessionshare.Key with the interface Shares: Create, List, Stop and StopAll. The methods that manage the relay address, the owner's relay identity, plugin capabilities, the relay's audit trail and the two relay tests have no counterpart because there is no relay; tier and fork changes have none because a viewer cannot act. Audit is a local table read by the list page.

Final verdict after reading the note: it decides how the browser Preview boots (from the shipped profile, with lazy chunks fetched on demand and Node's internal module interfaces emulated in the worker). Every part of it presupposes a JavaScript host running in a Web Worker. The owner dropped the in-browser runtime, so there is nothing for the decision to apply to; the first verdict is confirmed and now links to the owner's decision.

Final verdict after reading the note: change. Kept: the owner's host renders the viewer's page and decides every request, one access decision both draws and enforces, the feature is off by default, and a share whose state cannot be established is never driven. Replaced: the relay and its organization sign-in by a one-time invitation on the owner's own listener. Dropped: both driving tiers (the note itself says a view share is not watch-only), forks and their ceilings, viewer uploads and the owner state files. The first verdict 'ported' assumed a relay would still exist.

Final verdict after reading the note: drop, overturning the first verdict 'ported'. The note chooses the live method registry as the one list of plugin methods a share may expose. In the Go design a viewer may use four read actions on one session and nothing else, and a plugin is a separate process that registers no UI route, so there is no plugin method to expose and no catalog to enumerate. The note's principle, that what can be granted is read from the host's own registry and never from a plugin's declaration, is what the route registry already enforces.

Final verdict after reading the note: replace. The claim file exists so that two hosts on one home do not move each other's relay registrations and stop the owner's turn. The Go design has no relay registration and no durable share state: a share lives in the memory of the process whose listener serves it and ends with that process. A second host on the same home reads the audit rows, shows the badge read-only and cannot change a share it does not serve, which keeps the note's rule that contention is a visible answer and never a silent takeover.

Upstream lets the owner omit the lifetime, and such a share never expires. In the Go design the end time is a required field with a default of one hour and a configured ceiling, it is enforced by the binding's clock check at every decision and by a timer, and a host restart ends every share.

Upstream's lowest tier still lets a viewer prompt the session and stop its turn, so an owner who wants a passive viewer must rely on the viewer's restraint. The Go design has one role with four read actions; no route that sends input is in it, and a sweep of the route table proves the refusal.

The limit exists because a relay sits between viewer and owner and must assert who the viewer is outside a body it cannot read. With no relay, the principal is fixed by the owner's host from the cookie of the admitted connection, never from request data, and there is no frame to refuse.

The registration tokens, the unversioned owner-to-worker messages and the optional actor fields all serve a gateway worker process that keeps registrations at a relay. The Go design starts no worker and registers nowhere, so none of these identities or compatibility capabilities exist.

Authority snapshots are needed because the access list, mode and expiry are held by the relay and must be copied to the owner, versioned and cleared on socket loss. In the Go design the only copy of a share is the registry in the owner's host; the access decision reads it directly and fails closed when it cannot.

The unverified support for historical releases concerns a wire protocol between independently deployed owner and relay. No such protocol exists in the Go design: the viewer's browser receives HTML from the same binary that enforces the share, so there are no two versions to keep compatible.

Three separately shipped parts (owner, viewer page, Liveshare server) had to match versions. The Go design has one part: the owner's host renders the viewer's page and no server stands between them, so a version mismatch cannot arise.

Upstream accepts as a risk that any admitted viewer may attach files to the session. The view role does not contain the upload action, so a viewer's upload is refused before the handler runs; the owner has nothing to switch off.

The path check that a symlink swap can race, the list of tools a viewer's turn may run and the run_code program that the share does not bound all exist because a viewer starts turns. In the Go design a viewer starts no turn, so no tool ever runs on a viewer's behalf and there is no grant root to confine.

The Go viewer also has no file preview and no terminal: the file and terminal routes are outside the view role. The second half of the bullet does not carry over, because no installed-plugin method is exposed to a viewer.
justification: Kept on purpose. The file routes can read any file the session's filesystem backend allows, including paths outside the workspace, and a terminal is command execution as the operating-system user; neither can be made safe for a second person by a role alone. A viewer who needs a file asks the owner. Revisiting it would be a new decision together with a driving role.

reason: The missing dialog entry for adding sessions and the reload that returns to the first source both come from a share that carries several sessions. A Go share names exactly one session and its link opens that session, so there is no second source to add or to lose on reload; another session is another share.

The one-workspace rule keeps all sources of a multi-session share inside one granted workspace root, which matters because viewer turns run file tools there. A Go share has one session and grants no file access, so no workspace constraint is needed.

Upstream exposes installed plugins' remote methods to viewers with no sandbox and no read or write classification, trusting plugin code that runs inside the host. The Go design exposes no plugin method to a viewer, and a plugin is a separate process that registers no UI route, so the trust question does not arise.

The share-wide method selection with no per-viewer levels, and selections that outlive the catalog, belong to the plugin-method picker. No picker and no stored selection exist in the Go design; and because each share has exactly one viewer, every grant is per viewer by construction.

Upstream's reference picker answers a viewer from the whole session index and so discloses the id, title and directory path of every session on the host. The view role contains neither the completion action nor the session list, the viewer's page has no composer, and a list route cannot register without applying the access filter, so a viewer learns of no session but the shared one.

A method classified as readable but unreachable, because it names no session for the access check to bind, cannot exist in the Go route contract: every access-controlled id is a declared path parameter or the route does not register. The viewer's page has no composer, so the file picker the method feeds is not offered at all.

The late removal concerns the workspace feed a viewer's page renders. A Go viewer holds no global or workspace binding and is served no workspace or session list, so there is no feed to go stale; when a share ends the access change itself ends the viewer's streams.

The advisory claim file and per-registry snapshots exist because durable share state and relay registrations are addressed by the home directory while several hosts may serve it. A Go share is memory of the one process whose listener serves it; the only durable data are audit rows written in database transactions, and another host on the home reads them without being able to change a share.

Upstream checks authorization inside each share operation and publishes no separate observer of the invariant. In the Go design authorization is one decision made before any handler runs, from a rule every route must declare, and a test sweeps the whole route table as a viewer principal to prove that nothing outside the role is reachable.

Re-registration after a worker restart, reconnect loops stopped by relay refusals and credentials presented on restore are all behaviour of the gateway worker and its relay registration. Neither exists. A viewer's stream resumes by cursor through the ordinary event stream, and a host restart simply ends the share.

The split between admission and fork or write authority, the missing per-viewer execution levels, cancellation that cannot undo writes and the rule about which running turn a lapsed grant stops all follow from viewers who start turns. A Go viewer starts and stops nothing, so ending a share never has a turn to attribute or cancel and the owner's work is never touched.

The bullet is a release gate of the upstream build process: its assembled viewer artifact and SDK snapshots still need a final verification. The Go design has no assembled client artifact; its own acceptance is the real-browser scenarios of this specification.

Reads that bypass the carrier reach the relay instead of the owner, and root-absolute links break under the relay's path prefix. With no carrier and no relay every request of the viewer's browser goes to the owner's host, whose pages use document-relative references.

The hand-kept rule tables decide which npm package files enter the browser image. They exist only because a JavaScript host is packed for a Web Worker; the in-browser runtime is not built, and a Go binary's contents are decided by the compiler.

Reachability is inferred from the exact textual forms of JavaScript import and require calls, and misses computed ones. This is a property of packing dynamically loaded JavaScript modules; Go resolves imports at compile time and no image is packed.
The exclusion of vendored TypeScript sources is a choice about the contents of the npm-derived browser image. There is no image and no vendored TypeScript in the Go design.

The packer copies built lib/ artifacts and cannot tell that the workspace build is stale. That is an ordering hazard of upstream's multi-step JavaScript build; the Go build produces the binary from source in one step and nothing is packed afterwards.

The packer's command only works from inside a complete built upstream checkout because it reads the CLI source, config trees and fixtures by relative path. The command has no counterpart: the in-browser runtime and its build tool are not built.
The restriction to raw JSONL session inputs applies to fixtures packed into Preview overlays. No Preview fixture is packed, and the Go design reads no upstream session format in its store.

The worker writes uncompressed session logs because it carries no Zstandard codec for JavaScript in a browser. The in-browser runtime is not built, and the Go host stores sessions in a SQLite database, not in compressed log files.

Six Node built-in modules are stubs that throw, because a browser has no DNS resolver, sockets, processes or SQLite for JavaScript to call. They exist only to let Node-targeted code load in a Web Worker; the Go host runs on an operating system and uses the standard library.
The partial re-implementation of node:assert/strict is part of the Node emulation layer for the browser worker. No Node module is emulated in the Go design.
A browser worker cannot bind a TLS listener, so the emulated node:https refuses to start one. The Go host always runs as a process and serves TLS itself when the operator configures it.

Desktop product telemetry cannot be sent from the worker because its HTTP client is excluded from the browser image. The limit belongs to a host that is not built; in the Go design there is no desktop application, and telemetry is an opt-in sender owned by the host area.

The Preview cannot run pnpm or install plugins because a browser worker cannot start a package manager. The limit is specific to the browser-hosted JavaScript host; the Go design installs plugins from local directories and runs no package manager at all.

The Pi coding agent is replaced by a stand-in in the browser image because its native command and terminal dependencies cannot run in a worker. The stand-in exists only for the in-browser runtime; external agent runtimes on the real host are a separate area's subject.

Model requests are unavailable in the Preview: a stand-in for the provider library registers identifiers and refuses inference. This is a limit of the browser-hosted JavaScript host only; the Go host makes model requests through its own adapters.

Programs written for programmatic tool calling cannot run in the worker because it has no Node executable. The limit is specific to the in-browser runtime; the Go design has no guest runtime and scripts call tools through the tool command line.

Office conversion is refused in the Preview because the LibreOffice kit and its engine are excluded from the browser image. The limit belongs to a host that is not built; on the Go host conversion uses an operator-installed LibreOffice.

Hot module replacement replaces no modules in the worker because its module cache stays empty. It concerns reloading JavaScript modules in the browser-hosted host; the Go design never reloads code, only configuration.

Only some members of Node's internal module loader are emulated, so patching the CommonJS loader has no effect in the worker. This is a detail of imitating Node's internals in a browser and has no Go counterpart.

The emulated require('stream') returns a module namespace where Node returns a constructor, which breaks some CommonJS packages at load. It is an inaccuracy of the Node emulation layer, which the Go design does not have.

A lazily fetched file cannot be read synchronously before its archive is downloaded into the in-memory file system. The lazy archives and the in-memory file system exist only in the browser-hosted runtime.

File watchers see only the mounted in-memory file system, and the ref-counting calls cannot keep a worker alive. Both follow from emulating Node's fs watchers in a browser; the Go host watches the real file system through its watch service.

In the worker, confinement is a check inside the emulated file system and not kernel Landlock. The limit is specific to a host with no operating system beneath it; the Go host spawns commands under a real sandbox backend or does not run them.

The worker bundle pins a private file inside an npm package to keep an unused parser out of the browser download. It is an npm bundling workaround for the in-browser runtime and has no counterpart in a Go binary.

The worker's shell is a small interpreter with no loops, functions or job control and a table of core utilities, because a browser has no shell to run. The Go host runs the machine's real shell in a sandboxed process.

An emulated shell process reaches the in-memory file system only by messages, one round trip per entry, because the hosting site cannot grant the isolation that shared memory needs. Real processes on a real file system have neither the cost nor the interleaving.
The unmet coverage gate concerns the worker transport, the worker host and the page half, which need a browser to test. Those modules are not built, so no coverage is owed for them.
